{{Short description|Function in actuarial science}}
In [[actuarial science]] and [[demography]], '''force of mortality''', also known as '''death intensity''',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Andersen |first=Per Kragh |last2=Borgan |first2=Ørnulf |last3=Hjort |first3=Nils Lid |last4=Arjas |first4=Elja |last5=Stene |first5=Jon |last6=Aalen |first6=Odd |date=1985 |title=Counting Process Models for Life History Data: A Review [with Discussion and Reply] |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4615980 |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Statistics |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=97–158 |issn=0303-6898}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ioannidis |first=John P. A. |date=2013 |title=Expressing Death Risk as Condensed Life Experience and Death Intensity |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0272989X13484389 |journal=Medical Decision Making |language=en |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=853–859 |doi=10.1177/0272989X13484389 |issn=0272-989X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is a function, usually written <math>\mu(x)</math>, that gives the instantaneous rate at which deaths occur at age ''x'', conditional on survival to age ''x''.<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013" /> In [[survival analysis]] it corresponds to the [[hazard function]], and in [[reliability theory]] it corresponds to the [[failure rate]].<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003" /><ref name="RausandHoyland-Reliability-2004" /> It has units of inverse time, and integrating it over an interval gives the survival probability over that interval.<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003" />

==Definition==

Let <math>X</math> be a non-negative [[random variable]] representing an individual's age at death (or lifetime). Write <math>F(x)=\Pr(X\le x)</math> for its [[cumulative distribution function]] and <math>S(x)=\Pr(X>x)</math> for its [[survival function]].<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003"/>

The force of mortality at age <math>x</math>, written <math>\mu(x)</math>, is defined as the instantaneous conditional rate of death at age <math>x</math>. Formally, it is the limit of the [[conditional probability]] of dying in a short interval after <math>x</math>, divided by the interval length<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013"/>:
<math display="block">\mu(x)=\lim_{\Delta x\to 0^+}\frac{\Pr(x<X\le x+\Delta x\mid X>x)}{\Delta x}.</math>

When <math>X</math> is continuous with [[probability density function]] <math>f(x)</math>, the force of mortality can be written in terms of <math>f</math> and <math>S</math> as<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003"/>
<math display="block">\mu(x)=\frac{f(x)}{S(x)}=\frac{f(x)}{1-F(x)}.</math>

Equivalently, where <math>S</math> is differentiable, it is the negative derivative of the log-survival function<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003"/>:
<math display="block">\mu(x)=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\ln S(x).</math>

==Interpretation and related quantities==

The force of mortality <math>\mu(x)</math> is an instantaneous rate rather than a probability. For a short interval <math>\Delta x</math>, the conditional probability of dying shortly after age <math>x</math> is approximately <math>\mu(x)\,\Delta x</math>, provided <math>\Delta x</math> is small enough that the rate does not change much over the interval.<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013"/>

In survival analysis, <math>\mu(x)</math> is the [[hazard function]].<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003" /> In reliability theory, the same [[mathematical object]] is commonly called the [[failure rate]].<ref name="RausandHoyland-Reliability-2004"/>

The cumulative force of mortality (also called the cumulative hazard) is the integral of the force over age. Writing
<math display="block">H(x)=\int_0^x \mu(u)\,\mathrm{d}u</math>
then the survival function can be expressed as<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003"/>
<math display="block">S(x)=\exp\!\bigl(-H(x)\bigr).</math>

These identities imply the differential relationship
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}S(x)=-\mu(x)\,S(x)</math>
and, for a continuous lifetime distribution, the density can be written as<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003"/>
<math display="block">f(x)=\mu(x)\,S(x).</math>

==Survival probabilities and life tables==

In [[actuarial notation]], the probability that a life aged <math>x</math> survives for a further <math>t</math> years is written <math>{}_tp_x</math>. In terms of the lifetime random variable <math>X</math>, it is<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013"/>
<math display="block">{}_tp_x=\Pr(X>x+t\mid X>x)=\frac{S(x+t)}{S(x)}.</math>

Using the force of mortality, this conditional survival probability can be expressed as an exponential of the integrated force<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013" /><ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003" />:
<math display="block">{}_tp_x=\exp\!\left(-\int_x^{x+t}\mu(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\right).</math>

Life tables often tabulate survival and death probabilities at integer ages. In that setting, the one-year survival probability is <math>p_x={}_1p_x</math> and the one-year death probability is <math>q_x=1-p_x</math>.<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013" /> The force of mortality provides a continuous-age description that can be used to relate probabilities over different intervals through the integral relationship above.<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013" />

==Examples of mortality models==

Several parametric models are used to describe how the force of mortality varies with age. A constant force of mortality, <math>\mu(x)=\lambda</math> for <math>\lambda>0</math>, corresponds to an [[exponential distribution]] for <math>X</math> and gives a memoryless survival pattern.<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003" />

In actuarial work, the [[Gompertz–Makeham law of mortality]] is often written as the sum of an age-independent component and an exponentially increasing component, for example
<math display="block">\mu(x)=A+B\,c^x</math>
with <math>A\ge 0</math>, <math>B>0</math>, and <math>c>1</math>.<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013" /> The Gompertz model is the special case <math>A=0</math>, giving:<ref name="DicksonHardyWaters-LCR-2013" />
<math display="block">\mu(x)=B\,c^x</math>

A common model in survival analysis and reliability uses a [[Weibull distribution|Weibull]] hazard, which has the form
<math display="block">\mu(x)=\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}</math>
for shape <math>k>0</math> and scale <math>\lambda>0</math>. This family includes decreasing, constant, and increasing forces of mortality depending on the value of <math>k</math>.<ref name="KleinMoeschberger-Survival-2003" /><ref name="RausandHoyland-Reliability-2004" />
